title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
1. Introduction
Ancient DNA1 has transformed the study of third-millennium BCE mobility2 because it can test whether changes in ancestry accompanied archaeological transitions across Eurasia. Genome-wide ancestry estimates3, identity-by-descent segments4, kinship5, uniparental markers6 and isotope data7 can reveal population relationships and help distinguish long-distance movement from local continuity. These methods are particularly relevant to the Yamnaya horizon8, whose expansion began near the start of the project’s 3300–2600 BCE interval and was followed by major demographic changes both west and east of the Pontic–Caspian Steppe9. The evidence reviewed here supports a broad model of rapid, bidirectional dispersal10 of Yamnaya-related populations after a multi-stage formation process, followed by regionally variable admixture11 and restructuring rather than a single uniform replacement event (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2021).
1 DNA recovered from human remains, such as bones or teeth, dating to the past.2 Here, mobility means the movement of individuals or populations between regions.3 Estimates based on DNA markers across the whole genome that indicate which earlier populations contributed to a person’s ancestry.4 Stretches of DNA shared by people because they inherited them from a relatively recent common ancestor.5 Biological relationships among individuals, such as parent–child or siblings.6 Genetic markers inherited through only one parental line: mitochondrial DNA through the maternal line and the Y chromosome through the paternal line.7 Chemical signatures in teeth or bones that can provide clues about where a person grew up or what they ate.8 A widely distributed Early Bronze Age archaeological phenomenon associated with pastoral communities of the Pontic–Caspian Steppe.9 The grassland region north of the Black Sea and Caspian Sea.10 Movement in two directions—westward into Europe and eastward into Inner Asia.11 The genetic mixing of previously separated populations.12 The boundaries on what the evidence can reasonably demonstrate.13 An estimate of ancestry produced by comparing ancient genomes with selected reference populations.14 The study of how languages change over time and how different languages are historically related.15 Carefully qualified wording that reflects the strength and limits of the available evidence.The inferential limits12 of this evidence are equally important. Ancient genomes directly record biological relationships and modelled ancestry13, not ethnicity, archaeological identity or spoken language. Genetic results can therefore establish that a population moved, mixed or was replaced, while the connection of those processes to Indo-European language dispersal remains an interdisciplinary interpretation. Archaeological context and historical linguistics14 are required to assess whether a demographic expansion also transmitted language. Accordingly, this review distinguishes direct genetic observations from demographic interpretation and then from linguistic inference. It uses calibrated language15 such as “compatible with” or “consistent with” rather than claiming that DNA proves which language an individual spoke (Haak et al., 2015; Tassi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
section: 2. Evidence for Yamnaya population movement across Eurasia
text:
2. Evidence for Yamnaya population movement across Eurasia

2.1 Formation followed by expansion
Evidence immediately preceding 3300 BCE suggests that Yamnaya ancestry did not arise from an isolated or genetically uniform source. Lazaridis et al. (2025) modelled a multi-stage process in which Caucasus–Lower Volga-related ancestry moved west and mixed with Dnipro–Don hunter-gatherer-related ancestry, producing most of the ancestry later found in sampled Yamnaya individuals. Their reconstruction places the formation of a core population before the archaeological expansion and the rapid dispersal after approximately 3300 BCE. Nikitin et al. (2025) provide a complementary North Pontic sequence: Caucasus–Lower Volga-related migrants mixed with Trypillian farmers16 in the formation of Usatove groups, while a parallel mixture with local foragers17 contributed to Serednii Stih populations, from which later Yamnaya groups derived substantial ancestry. Chintalapati et al. (2022), using admixture-date estimates18 across Europe and western Asia, likewise place important Steppe-ancestry formation processes before the archaeological appearance of the Yamnaya and Afanasievo horizons19. These models converge on staged formation followed by expansion, although they do not yet resolve one precise formation centre or every intervening route.
16 Farming communities associated with the Cucuteni–Trypillia archaeological culture of eastern Europe.17 People who obtained food mainly through hunting, fishing and gathering rather than farming.18 Statistical estimates of approximately when two previously distinct populations began mixing.19 The Afanasievo horizon was an Early Bronze Age archaeological phenomenon in the Altai and nearby parts of Inner Asia.Earlier southeastern European evidence provides necessary context but should not be treated as direct evidence for the 3300–2600 BCE migration itself. Mathieson et al. (2018) identified intermittent genetic contact between Steppe and southeastern European populations long before the large third-millennium BCE ancestry shifts. This longer history indicates that the Yamnaya expansion emerged from existing networks of contact rather than initiating east–west interaction. However, the rapidity and scale of the later dispersal distinguish it from these earlier contacts. The chronological distinction is therefore between earlier interaction that contributed to ancestry formation, the Yamnaya expansion beginning around 3300 BCE, and subsequent regional transformations within and after the target interval (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Mathieson et al., 2018; Nikitin et al., 2025).


2.2 Westward movement into Europe
The strongest evidence for Yamnaya-related migration is the large ancestry shift in central and northern Europe near 3000 BCE. Haak et al. (2015) estimated that sampled German Corded Ware20 individuals derived approximately three-quarters of their ancestry from a Yamnaya-related source, a result inconsistent with an explanation based only on the circulation of artefacts or ideas. Allentoft et al. (2015) independently found substantial genetic affinity21 between Yamnaya and Corded Ware groups across their broader Eurasian dataset. More recently, Ringbauer et al. (2024) identified long identity-by-descent segments linking several Corded Ware and Yamnaya groups. Because such long segments indicate relatively recent shared ancestors, these results narrow the demographic connection to only a few hundred years and strengthen the case for rapid movement from the Steppe into central and northern Europe (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015; Ringbauer et al., 2024).
20 An archaeological phenomenon of third-millennium BCE Europe named after the cord impressions used to decorate pottery.21 Genetic similarity that suggests shared ancestry or historical population connections.This convergence does not mean that every Corded Ware community descended directly from one sampled Yamnaya population. Haak et al. (2015) acknowledged that their Samara Yamnaya sample might not be the precise source, while Ringbauer et al. (2024) identified both recent Yamnaya connections and substantial ancestry related to Globular Amphora populations. Papac et al. (2021) similarly found that Corded Ware groups in Bohemia possessed high but heterogeneous Steppe-related ancestry that could not be explained entirely by the sampled Yamnaya sources. “Yamnaya-related ancestry” is therefore more accurate than assuming descent from a single homogeneous Yamnaya group. The broad westward movement is strongly supported, but the contributing source populations, corridors and number of migration pulses remain less certain (Haak et al., 2015; Papac et al., 2021; Ringbauer et al., 2024).


2.3 Eastward movement into Inner Asia
Ancient DNA also supports an eastward expansion. Allentoft et al. (2015) found Afanasievo individuals from the Altai22 to be genetically close to sampled Yamnaya groups, consistent with rapid movement across a very large distance in the early third millennium BCE. Wang et al. (2021) extended this pattern into western Mongolia and Xinjiang, identifying Yamnaya/Afanasievo-related ancestry after approximately 3000 BCE. Their regional sequence shows that the ancestry later declined in parts of Mongolia while persisting farther west, demonstrating that eastward dispersal was followed by local admixture and population turnover23 rather than permanent demographic uniformity. Chintalapati et al. (2022) provide a broader chronological framework compatible with the formation and later spread of this ancestry.
22 A mountain region in Inner Asia where Russia, Mongolia, China and Kazakhstan meet.23 A substantial change in a region’s population through migration, replacement or mixing.The eastern evidence is less geographically continuous than the evidence from central Europe. Genetic similarity between Yamnaya and Afanasievo populations supports a broad eastward dispersal, but sparsely sampled intermediate areas limit reconstruction of the exact route. Archaeological labels also cannot substitute for ancestry: Wang et al. (2021) report that an Afanasievo-associated context did not invariably correspond to Yamnaya-related genetic ancestry. The most defensible conclusion is therefore that closely related populations moved east toward the Altai, western Mongolia and Xinjiang after about 3000 BCE, while the detailed corridors and correspondence between archaeological and genetic classifications remain provisional (Allentoft et al., 2015; Chintalapati et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
3. Routes, chronology and demographic consequences

3.1 A sequence rather than a single event
Across the evidence, Yamnaya-associated mobility is best understood as a sequence. Earlier mixtures in the Caucasus–Lower Volga, Dnipro–Don, North Pontic and southeastern European interaction zones supplied the ancestry and social connections from which expansion emerged. Direct target-period evidence then documents westward and eastward movement beginning around 3300–3000 BCE. Finally, regional studies record assimilation, further turnover and long-distance continuities during the later target period and after 2600 BCE (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Mathieson et al., 2018; Nikitin et al., 2025). This sequence prevents later transformations—particularly Bell Beaker-period changes—from being projected backwards as direct evidence about Yamnaya communities.
The Corded Ware relationship illustrates both the strength and uncertainty of route reconstruction. Genome-wide ancestry and identity-by-descent evidence support rapid, recent genealogical connections with Yamnaya-related populations, but the sampled Yamnaya groups need not represent the only source. Corded Ware populations also incorporated ancestry related to earlier European groups and differed between regions. The data therefore favour substantial population movement followed by local admixture over either a purely cultural diffusion model or a uniform replacement by one genetically homogeneous migrant population (Haak et al., 2015; Papac et al., 2021; Ringbauer et al., 2024).


3.2 Replacement, admixture and regional restructuring
Regional time series24 show that the demographic consequences of Steppe migration varied markedly. In Bohemia, Corded Ware populations appeared by approximately 2900 BCE with high but variable Steppe-related ancestry, after which the incorporation of women with diverse ancestry and sharp changes in Y-chromosome lineages25 indicate repeated social and genetic restructuring. Some of the most pronounced changes occurred around 2600 BCE or later, so they represent the end of the target interval and its consequences rather than the initial Yamnaya expansion (Papac et al., 2021). In southeastern Poland, genomic, kinship and strontium-isotope data26 instead reveal a smaller-scale pattern in which Steppe-associated paternal ancestry coexisted with maternal lineages27 related to earlier Neolithic populations, including kin relationships that crossed local and non-local mobility categories (Linderholm et al., 2020). Together, these studies replace a single model of “mass migration” with evidence for multiple combinations of long-distance movement, local incorporation and community reorganisation.
24 Genetic samples from the same region but from different periods, allowing researchers to track change over time.25 Lines of paternal descent traced through variants of the Y chromosome.26 Measurements of strontium in teeth that can help determine whether a person grew up locally or moved from another geological region.27 Lines of descent traced through mothers, commonly studied using mitochondrial DNA.28 A migration in which males and females participated in different proportions.29 Relating to the non-sex chromosomes, which are inherited from both parents.30 Relating to the X chromosome, whose inheritance pattern differs between males and females.31 The proportion and depth of an ancient genome successfully recovered through DNA sequencing.The migration was often sex-biased28, but its magnitude cannot be assumed to have been constant across Eurasia. Scorrano et al. (2021) found stronger male bias in Steppe-related ancestry among several Corded Ware groups than among Bell Beaker groups, using autosomal29, X-chromosomal30 and uniparental comparisons. Linderholm et al. (2020) and Papac et al. (2021) likewise identify patterns consistent with male-linked Steppe ancestry and the incorporation of local or genetically diverse women. Nevertheless, these conclusions are best resolved in parts of central Europe and southeastern Poland, and some estimates are limited by small sample sizes, uneven genome coverage31 and low X-chromosome marker counts. Sex-biased mobility is thus a recurring regional mechanism, not a securely quantified Eurasia-wide constant (Linderholm et al., 2020; Papac et al., 2021; Scorrano et al., 2021).
Later Bell Beaker evidence32 further demonstrates why archaeological culture and population movement must be separated. Olalde et al. (2018) found limited genetic affinity between Iberian and central European Beaker-associated groups, suggesting that some shared material practices spread without equivalent population movement. In Britain, by contrast, Beaker-associated migration introduced high Steppe-related ancestry and replaced approximately 90% of the existing gene pool33 within a few centuries. This British transformation mainly postdates 2600 BCE and is therefore a consequence of earlier Steppe-related dispersal rather than direct evidence for the initial Yamnaya migration. Tassi et al. (2017) provide a complementary earlier case: Globular Amphora34 individuals in northwestern Poland were genetically closer to earlier Neolithic populations and lacked the expected Yamnaya-derived profile despite eastern archaeological affinities. Taken together, these results show that material culture can spread through cultural transmission in one context and accompany major demographic change in another (Olalde et al., 2018; Tassi et al., 2017).
32 Evidence associated with the Bell Beaker phenomenon, named after its distinctive bell-shaped pottery.33 The total collection of genetic variation present in a population.34 A Late Neolithic archaeological culture of central and eastern Europe named after its rounded pottery vessels.

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
4. Migration and Indo-European language dispersal

4.1 A compatible demographic mechanism
The scale and speed of Yamnaya-related movement provide a credible demographic mechanism through which languages could have dispersed. Haak et al. (2015) interpreted the major Steppe-derived ancestry influx into central Europe as support for a Steppe-origin model for at least some Indo-European languages, while explicitly acknowledging that genetic data are silent about the language spoken by sampled individuals. Allentoft et al. (2015) similarly described the bidirectional genomic transformations of Bronze Age Eurasia as consistent with a proposed early Bronze Age dispersal of Indo-European languages. These conclusions are meaningful because large movements of people create opportunities for language transmission, but they do not demonstrate that population replacement and language replacement occurred at the same rate or through the same social process.
The reviewed studies vary in how directly they discuss language. Some make explicit linguistic interpretations of their demographic results, whereas others supply indirect evidence about migration chronology, scale, sex bias or social incorporation. The latter studies should not be presented as independent confirmation of a linguistic hypothesis. For example, identity-by-descent links between Yamnaya and Corded Ware groups strengthen the evidence for recent population movement, but do not identify the language of either group (Ringbauer et al., 2024). Likewise, sex-biased ancestry and kinship structures may help reconstruct how migrants were incorporated, but they cannot show which languages were used within households or transmitted to later generations (Linderholm et al., 2020; Papac et al., 2021; Scorrano et al., 2021).


4.2 Eastward dispersal and the proto-Tocharian interpretation
The eastward Yamnaya–Afanasievo connection has particular relevance to proposals concerning proto-Tocharian35. Wang et al. (2021) argue that the movement of a population closely related to Yamnaya into the Altai and farther into Inner Asia adds weight to a migration-mediated account of proto-Tocharian dispersal. Allentoft et al. (2015) and Chintalapati et al. (2022) provide supporting demographic and chronological context for this eastward movement. However, “proto-Tocharian” is a linguistic interpretation applied to the demographic pattern, not a genetic measurement. Sparse sampling along intermediate routes and the imperfect correspondence between Afanasievo archaeological contexts and Yamnaya-related ancestry make a one-to-one mapping between population movement and language branch unjustified (Allentoft et al., 2015; Chintalapati et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2021).
35 The reconstructed ancestor of the extinct Tocharian languages once spoken in parts of the Tarim Basin.36 A proposed ancestral stage before the Anatolian languages separated from the other Indo-European branches.Broader proposals about Indo-European roots require the same caution. Lazaridis et al. (2025) connect their reconstruction of Caucasus–Lower Volga and North Pontic ancestry formation to a model of proto-Indo-Anatolian unity36 before Yamnaya expansion and later language branching. This is the collection’s most explicit integration of genetic, archaeological and linguistic reasoning, but the linguistic conclusion remains dependent on the demographic model and independent linguistic assumptions. The unresolved location of some source populations and routes, including proposed connections towards Anatolia, prevents genetic models alone from determining a language homeland. Tassi et al. (2017) reinforce this limitation from the opposite direction: an archaeological group can display eastern cultural affinities without the expected Steppe ancestry, and language change need not follow demographic movement exactly. Genetic evidence can therefore test whether a proposed language-spread model has a plausible population mechanism, but it cannot adjudicate language identity by itself (Lazaridis et al., 2025; Tassi et al., 2017).

section: 5. Limits of linking genes, archaeological culture and language
text:
5. Limits of linking genes, archaeological culture and language
The broad directions of Yamnaya-related movement are more secure than their fine-grained routes. Ancient-DNA models depend on the populations available as ancestry proxies37, and unsampled groups may have contributed to both Yamnaya and Corded Ware populations. Admixture-date methods can also compress several closely spaced movements into an approximate date, while identity-by-descent detection depends on genome coverage and performs most reliably for longer segments. These constraints do not overturn the evidence for rapid dispersal, but they limit claims about a single point of origin, a unique migration corridor or an exact number of pulses38 (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Nikitin et al., 2025; Ringbauer et al., 2024).
37 Sampled populations used as stand-ins when estimating the ancestry of another population.38 Separate episodes or waves of migration.39 A sequence of samples collected across a geographic route or a series of locations.The evidence is geographically and chronologically uneven. Central and northern Europe contain comparatively dense regional and community-level datasets, whereas the lower Volga, North Pontic–Caucasus zones, northern Eurasia and intermediate Inner Asian corridors remain less continuously sampled. Research using modern northern Eurasian genomes and published ancient comparators provides context for older Siberian–European interactions, but cannot substitute for a direct transect39 of Yamnaya-period individuals (Wong et al., 2017). Similarly, studies spanning millennia must isolate the 3300–2600 BCE evidence from earlier ancestry formation and later Bronze Age consequences. Without this separation, later replacement or modern-population affinity can be mistaken for direct evidence about Yamnaya migration (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Mathieson et al., 2018; Olalde et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2017).
Most importantly, ancestry, archaeological culture, ethnicity and language are distinct analytical categories. An individual may be buried in a Corded Ware or Afanasievo context without possessing a uniform ancestry profile, and a population may adopt material practices without large-scale genetic change. Conversely, a substantial ancestry shift demonstrates migration but does not reveal whether incoming languages replaced, coexisted with or were adopted by local populations. None of the genetic studies reviewed contains a direct linguistic dataset capable of testing speech, branching, borrowing or multilingualism. Ancient DNA can therefore support or constrain demographic scenarios associated with Indo-European dispersal, but the linguistic argument ultimately requires independent historical-linguistic and archaeological evidence (Tassi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
6. Synthesis and research gaps
Ancient DNA provides strong evidence that Yamnaya-related mobility was a major Eurasian demographic process during 3300–2600 BCE. The most coherent reconstruction is a multi-stage formation process involving interaction among Caucasus–Lower Volga-related, Dnipro–Don/North Pontic and neighbouring populations, followed by rapid expansion from approximately 3300 BCE. Westward movement into central and northern Europe is supported by large ancestry shifts and recent genealogical links, while the genetic relationship between Yamnaya and Afanasievo populations supports a parallel eastward movement towards the Altai and Inner Asia. In both directions, migration was followed by regionally different mixtures of incorporation, sex bias, continuity and replacement rather than a single uniform process (Allentoft et al., 2015; Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Nikitin et al., 2025; Papac et al., 2021; Ringbauer et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2021).
Several questions remain unresolved. Direct sampling is still insufficient to define every lower-Volga, North Pontic, Caucasus or possible Anatolian route, and intermediate populations between the Pontic–Caspian Steppe and Inner Asia remain sparse. Source substructure40 and chronological resolution41 make it difficult to distinguish one large migration from several closely spaced movements. Community-level studies of kinship, mobility and sex bias are concentrated in a limited number of European settings, restricting comparison across Eurasia. More matched archaeological–genetic transects are needed to determine when similar material cultures reflect population movement, local adoption or mixed processes (Chintalapati et al., 2022; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Linderholm et al., 2020; Nikitin et al., 2025; Papac et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021).
40 Genetic differences among smaller groups within what might otherwise be treated as one source population.41 How precisely the available evidence can distinguish events occurring at different times.The largest interpretive gap concerns language. The demographic expansion is compatible with some Steppe-based models of Indo-European dispersal and supplies a plausible mechanism for moving languages across large distances. It does not, however, establish the speech of Yamnaya, Corded Ware or Afanasievo individuals, nor does it independently resolve language homelands, branches or transmission mechanisms. The defensible conclusion is therefore two-part: ancient DNA strongly supports rapid bidirectional dispersal of Yamnaya-related populations and subsequent regional restructuring, while any connection between those movements and particular Indo-European languages remains an interdisciplinary inference rather than a direct genetic finding (Haak et al., 2015; Lazaridis et al., 2025; Tassi et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2021).

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
1. Defining the problem

1.1 Scope and boundaries

Focus on population movement across Eurasia during 3300–2600 BCE and its possible relationship to language dispersal.
Distinguish evidence that falls directly within the target period from earlier evidence concerning population formation and later evidence concerning demographic consequences.
Discuss origins, archaeological culture and genetic formation only where they contribute to the migration and language argument.



1.2 Types of evidence and their limits

Ancient genomes, ancestry models, identity-by-descent analysis, kinship studies, uniparental markers and relevant isotope evidence provide the main evidence for population movement.5
Migration, admixture and replacement are demographic interpretations drawn from these data.
Archaeological evidence can help reconstruct the context and possible routes of movement, but similarities in material culture do not by themselves demonstrate migration.
Linguistic conclusions require a further interpretive step because language cannot be observed directly in ancient DNA.

5 will I be able to Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 10 and 17; Synthesis Table columns L–M.

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
2. Evidence for Yamnaya population movement

2.1 Population formation before the main expansion

Reconstruct the stages through which Steppe-related ancestry formed before the rapid expansion associated with Yamnaya populations around 3300 BCE.
Compare Lazaridis et al. (2025), Nikitin et al. (2025), Chintalapati et al. (2022) and Mathieson et al. (2018).
Use earlier contacts and ancestry formation only where they help explain the populations involved in the later expansion.
Retain uncertainty over the precise geographic centre of formation, the suitability of sampled groups as genetic proxies and the routes through which ancestry components were assembled.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 5 and 11; Synthesis Themes row 2.


2.2 Westward movement into Europe

Assess genetic evidence for substantial movement of Yamnaya-related populations into central and northern Europe around and after 3000 BCE.
Combine ancestry proportions, evidence of population turnover and identity-by-descent relationships rather than relying on a single form of genetic evidence.
Compare Haak et al. (2015), Allentoft et al. (2015), Ringbauer et al. (2024) and Papac et al. (2021).
Use the term “Yamnaya-related ancestry” where the evidence does not identify a particular sampled Yamnaya population as the direct source.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 6, 12 and 13; Synthesis Themes row 3.


2.3 Eastward movement into Inner Asia

Examine the close genetic relationship between Yamnaya-associated populations and Afanasievo-associated groups as evidence of eastward population movement after about 3000 BCE.
Trace the appearance of related ancestry toward the Altai, western Mongolia and Xinjiang.
Compare Wang et al. (2021), Allentoft et al. (2015) and Chintalapati et al. (2022).
Treat the intermediate migration routes as uncertain because direct sampling remains limited.
Avoid assuming that genetic populations correspond exactly to the archaeological category “Afanasievo.”

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 7, 15 and 19; Synthesis Themes row 5.

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
3. Routes, chronology and demographic effects

3.1 Chronological sequence

Organise the evidence into three periods: formation before 3300 BCE, migration during 3300–2600 BCE and later demographic consequences.
Do not use substantially later population replacement as if it were direct evidence for the Yamnaya-period migration itself.
Include broad genomic studies or studies based partly on modern populations only when they clarify events within the target-period sequence.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 16 and 23; Synthesis Table column K.


3.2 Corded Ware and the problem of identifying sources

Compare the high levels of Yamnaya-related ancestry in Corded Ware-associated populations with evidence of recent genealogical connections and source heterogeneity.
Avoid treating either Corded Ware groups or sampled Yamnaya populations as genetically homogeneous.
Distinguish evidence of demographic relationship from claims about language. Genetic proximity alone cannot establish that two populations spoke the same language.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps row 12; Synthesis Table rows 6–9.


3.3 Admixture, replacement and regional restructuring

Compare large ancestry shifts with evidence for continued local ancestry, repeated migration and incorporation of existing populations.
Use Haak et al. (2015), Papac et al. (2021), Linderholm et al. (2020) and Olalde et al. (2018) to show that the demographic effects of Steppe-related migration differed between regions.
Distinguish cases of major population turnover from cases in which incoming populations mixed extensively with local groups.
Do not apply estimates derived from Britain or central Europe to Eurasia as a whole.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 8 and 13; Synthesis Themes rows 3, 4 and 6.


3.4 Sex-biased migration and local mobility

Examine evidence for male-biased Steppe-related ancestry together with evidence for incorporation of local maternal lineages.
Use kinship and mobility studies to examine how migration operated at family and community levels.
Compare Scorrano et al. (2021), Linderholm et al. (2020) and Papac et al. (2021).
Treat sex-biased migration as a recurring pattern whose strength and form differed between regions.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 8, 14 and 21; Synthesis Themes row 4.


3.5 Cultural change and population movement

Compare cases of genetic continuity with cases of substantial ancestry replacement to show that changes in material culture need not reflect the same demographic process in every region.
Use Tassi et al. (2017), Olalde et al. (2018) and Papac et al. (2021) to distinguish cultural transmission from large-scale movement of people.
Keep later Bell Beaker evidence separate from direct evidence for migration during 3300–2600 BCE. Use it only to discuss later consequences of Steppe-related population movement.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 9 and 22; Synthesis Themes row 6.

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
section: 4. Yamnaya migration and Indo-European language dispersal
text:
4. Yamnaya migration and Indo-European language dispersal

4.1 Population movement as a possible mechanism of language dispersal

Assess whether rapid Steppe-related population movement provides a demographic mechanism consistent with particular models of Indo-European dispersal.
Separate three levels of argument: the genetic observation, the demographic interpretation and the linguistic inference.
Use cautious terms such as “compatible with,” “consistent with” and “interpreted by the authors as supporting.”
Do not treat genetic evidence for migration as direct evidence of language transmission.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 10 and 17; Synthesis Themes row 8.


4.2 Strength of linguistic claims in the literature

Distinguish the six studies that make explicit language claims from the seven that make indirect claims and the two that provide background evidence.
Avoid presenting all genetic studies as evidence for the same linguistic hypothesis.
Attribute claims about particular language families, branches or homelands to the authors who make them.
Give greater weight to genetic studies for demographic questions than for linguistic conclusions.

Workbook trace: Synthesis Themes cell G8; Synthesis Table columns L–M.


4.3 Eastward migration and proto-Tocharian interpretations

Use the eastward movement associated with Afanasievo-related populations as evidence for a demographic expansion into Inner Asia.
Examine the argument made by some authors that this movement is compatible with the dispersal of proto-Tocharian or ancestral Tocharian-speaking populations.
Emphasise the limited sampling of intermediate regions between the western Steppe and Inner Asia.
Treat the association with proto-Tocharian as a linguistic interpretation rather than a result measured genetically.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 7, 15 and 19.


4.4 Language origins and models of Yamnaya formation

Compare proposals concerning Proto-Indo-Anatolian or Steppe-associated language origins with the demographic sequence reconstructed from ancient DNA.
Examine whether proposed linguistic homelands correspond plausibly with the timing and geography of population formation and later migration.
Treat proposed language-root locations as interdisciplinary hypotheses.
Do not equate genetic ancestry components with languages, peoples or ethnic identities.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 11, 17 and 18; Synthesis Themes rows 2 and 8.

title: What can DNA analysis reveal about the migration patterns of the Yamnaya people across the Eurasian region from 3300 to 2600 BCE?
text:
5. Limits of the evidence

5.1 Uncertainty in migration routes and source populations

Explain how unsampled populations, the use of proxy sources, preservation bias and dependence on statistical models affect reconstructions of migration routes.
Distinguish broad patterns that are well supported from detailed routes or individual migration pulses that remain provisional.
Avoid assigning more geographic precision to ancestry models than the available samples allow.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 11–13, 18–19 and 23.


5.2 Uneven geographic and chronological sampling

Compare the relatively dense ancient-DNA record from Europe with weaker coverage in the Caucasus, lower Volga region, northern Eurasia and Inner Asia.
Consider how this imbalance affects confidence in reconstructions of eastward and intermediate migration routes.
Avoid assuming that migration mechanisms documented at European community level operated in the same way throughout Eurasia.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 16 and 18–21, 23.


5.3 Ancestry, archaeological culture and language are different categories

Keep genetic ancestry, archaeological culture, ethnicity and language analytically separate.
Use ancient DNA to investigate biological relationships, population movement, admixture and demographic change.
Use archaeological evidence to reconstruct cultural and material contexts.
Treat linguistic affiliation as a separate historical inference requiring linguistic as well as archaeological and genetic evidence.
Ancient DNA can test whether a proposed language-dispersal model is demographically plausible, but it cannot identify the language spoken by an ancient individual or prove language replacement.

Workbook trace: Agreements & Gaps rows 9–10, 17 and 24.
